Pregnancy

Mercury exposure during pregnancy: food, spills and everyday precautions

Updated: October 18, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Mercury exposure is not one single situation. Eating fish, breathing vapour from a broken device and using a contaminated cream involve different forms and routes. High exposure can harm health and a developing baby, but a past meal or the presence of an intact household item does not establish poisoning. The useful response is to identify the source, stop further exposure safely and obtain advice appropriate to the incident.

The form and route matter

Mercury can occur as a silvery liquid metal, inorganic compounds or organic forms such as methylmercury. Metallic mercury can release invisible, odourless vapour when exposed to air; inhaling it is an important route of absorption. Some inorganic compounds in skin products can also enter through skin. These routes cannot be assessed by smell or treated as interchangeable.

Natural processes and activities such as coal burning, waste incineration and mining release mercury into the environment. Microorganisms can convert mercury in water into methylmercury, which accumulates through aquatic food chains. Eating contaminated fish is the main methylmercury route for many people. Food, water, workplace contact and broken products therefore need different investigations.

Risk does not mean inevitable fetal harm

Effects depend on the chemical form, amount, route, duration and individual health. High exposure can affect the nervous system and kidneys; inhaled metallic mercury can also injure the lungs. Methylmercury can cross the placenta, and the developing nervous system is particularly vulnerable, including functions involved in movement, learning, hearing and vision.

These possible effects do not predict the outcome of every contact. Evidence for pregnancy outcomes after elemental or inorganic mercury exposure is more limited than for major methylmercury poisoning. Feeling well does not exclude an exposure, and symptoms alone cannot measure it. Describe the actual event to a clinician rather than assuming a baby has been harmed or that no assessment is needed.

Choose suitable fish rather than avoiding all seafood

Lower-mercury fish can supply useful pregnancy nutrients. As one regional example, US FDA/EPA advice is two to three four-ounce servings weekly from its Best Choices list, about 225–340 g in total, OR one four-ounce serving from Good Choices. These are alternative patterns, not allowances to add together; follow the guidance for your country and locally caught fish.

Examples of lower-mercury choices include salmon, shrimp, pollock and catfish. Canned light tuna is different from albacore/white tuna. The US Avoid list includes shark, swordfish, king mackerel, marlin, orange roughy, bigeye tuna and tilefish from the Gulf of Mexico. This does not mean all mackerel or all tilefish. Cooking does not remove mercury already in fish. Review repeated high-mercury intake with maternity care; one meal alone does not prove fetal injury.

Dental fillings need an individual dental decision

Amalgam is a mixture of metals containing elemental mercury and can release small amounts of vapour. Tell the dentist you are pregnant, planning pregnancy or breastfeeding. FDA advises considering non-amalgam materials for these groups when clinically suitable. Material choice depends on the tooth, alternatives, your health and applicable local practice; a filling does not by itself establish poisoning or a need for removal.

Do not arrange removal of an intact amalgam filling without decay solely to prevent mercury-related illness. Removal can temporarily increase vapour exposure and sacrifice healthy tooth. A broken filling, decay, allergy or other clinical problem needs dental assessment. Necessary dental care can be provided during pregnancy; do not postpone treatment for pain or infection out of fear.

Reduce breakage and identify older products

Some older thermometers, barometers, switches, novelty glass pendants, batteries and other devices contain mercury; many modern alternatives do not. Do not assume every silver-looking thermometer liquid is mercury-free. Check the label or manufacturer, choose a mercury-free replacement and store fragile devices safely away from children. An intact sealed device is a different exposure situation from a broken one.

Do not open, heat or dismantle suspect antiques or devices to check their contents. Arrange local hazardous-waste or recycling advice for unwanted mercury items, keeping them protected from breakage. Mercury-containing creams are a separate concern, often involving inorganic compounds rather than a visible pool of metal. A product can contain mercury without the user seeing silver droplets.

If a thermometer or other mercury device breaks

Keep people and pets away and avoid walking through the spill. Leave the area, close access to other rooms and ventilate to the outdoors if you can do so without further exposure. Do not use a vacuum cleaner or broom, pour mercury into a drain or carry contamination around on shoes or clothing. During pregnancy, stay out of cleanup and obtain local environmental, health or poison-service instructions.

A spill larger than a thermometer, an unknown quantity, contamination in cracks or absorbent material, or a spill already vacuumed needs specific professional advice. A non-pregnant adult should not improvise simply because they are not pregnant. Small-spill instructions depend on the surface and complete droplet recovery. Collected mercury, glass and cleanup materials need secure containment and locally approved disposal; putting them straight into an ordinary outside bin is not a universal safe solution.

Broken fluorescent bulbs have separate instructions

Fluorescent bulbs contain much less mercury than a mercury thermometer, and their broken glass and powder need bulb-specific handling. EPA advises leaving the room, airing it outdoors for 5–10 minutes and switching off central forced-air heating or cooling before cleanup. Do not begin by vacuuming. Keep the pregnant person, children and pets away while an appropriate adult follows the full instructions.

The recommended collection method and container depend on the surface; local rules determine disposal. Continue outside ventilation as advised, and ask for help if cleanup is uncertain. Thermometer guidance includes ventilation for at least 24 hours after successful cleanup; bulb guidance uses its own timetable. Do not treat a quick look at the floor or absence of smell as proof that all contamination has gone.

Review exposure at work and in skin products

Dental work, electrical or chemical manufacturing, mining, recycling and other jobs may involve mercury or other metals, but the job title alone does not establish exposure. Tell occupational health, the safety officer and your maternity clinician what materials and tasks are involved. Review ventilation, spill procedures, suitable protective equipment and any monitoring or task changes. Leave or reassignment is an individual risk-control decision, not an automatic rule for every worker.

Prevent carrying workplace contamination home on clothes and shoes, and follow workplace hygiene procedures before eating. Do not use unlabelled or suspect skin-lightening or anti-ageing products. If a product contains mercury, stop using it, wash affected skin and get medical advice. Family members may also contact contaminated towels or surfaces. Keep the product safely sealed for identification and disposal advice; do not share it or put it back into use.

Get an exposure assessment, not a home detox

After skin contamination, avoid spreading it, remove contaminated clothing and wash affected skin with lukewarm water and soap for 10–15 minutes. For eye exposure, remove contact lenses and rinse with lukewarm water for 10–15 minutes while arranging medical advice. Leave contaminated air rather than staying to finish cleanup. If you may have inhaled or swallowed mercury, seek immediate medical or poison-service advice.

Tell the team the product, time, amount if known, room ventilation, any cleanup already attempted, symptoms and pregnancy stage. Blood, urine or other tests are chosen according to the suspected form and timing; a test result alone cannot predict the baby’s outcome. Routine testing after every fish meal is not recommended. Do not induce vomiting or use detox supplements, chelation products or home test kits to choose treatment; any specialist treatment must be individually supervised.

When the situation needs emergency care

If you think you have been poisoned, obtain emergency assessment now, even before symptoms appear. If unsure whether a substance or contact was harmful, contact a poison service or urgent medical service immediately for triage. New cough, chest discomfort, breathlessness, vomiting, tremor, altered sensation or visual changes after a credible exposure need prompt advice rather than waiting for the next antenatal visit.

Call emergency services for severe breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, or marked confusion or rapidly worsening illness. Do not drive yourself, re-enter contaminated air or delay care to collect spilled material. A photo or intact package can help identify the substance if safely available. While waiting after suspected acute poisoning, do not give food or drink or try to make the person vomit unless the treating service directs otherwise.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Record the source, route, time and cleanup already attempted, and ask your maternity clinician or poison service what assessment is needed.

Use local fish advice, review dental and workplace options with the relevant professionals, and replace fragile mercury devices safely.

Keep away from spills, follow device-specific public-health cleanup and disposal instructions, and obtain immediate help for suspected poisoning instead of using a home detox.

How BeMama can help

A practical plan separates dietary choices from household or workplace incidents. Keeping product details and asking the right service for advice is more useful than assuming that every exposure has the same risk or trying to remove mercury yourself.

When to seek help

Leave a contaminated area and seek immediate advice after possible harmful exposure; suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment even if symptoms have not started. Severe breathing difficulty, seizures, fainting or loss of consciousness, marked confusion or rapid deterioration need emergency services. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting or enter the spill area to collect evidence. Never vacuum mercury or use unsupervised detox or chelation products. Follow local cleanup and disposal instructions.

Evidence notes updated: October 18, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Mercury form, amount, route and duration determine the assessment; exposure is not automatic proof of fetal harm.
  • Use local lower-mercury fish advice and keep the nutritional benefits of suitable seafood.
  • Discuss new dental filling materials, while preserving intact fillings unless removal is clinically needed.
  • Never vacuum a mercury spill; isolate the area and follow the correct device-specific cleanup and disposal advice.
  • Seek immediate advice for possible harmful exposure and emergency care for suspected poisoning or severe symptoms; avoid home detox.

Frequently asked questions

How much fish can I eat during pregnancy?

Use one local guideline. US FDA/EPA advice is two to three four-ounce servings weekly from Best Choices, or one four-ounce serving from Good Choices, without adding the two allowances. Species matter: canned light and white/albacore tuna are different. Check local catch advisories and discuss repeated high-mercury intake rather than banning all fish.

Does an amalgam filling mean I have mercury poisoning?

No. It contains elemental mercury, but having a filling does not diagnose poisoning. Discuss pregnancy and suitable materials for new treatment. FDA does not recommend removing intact fillings without decay solely for prevention, because removal adds temporary exposure and loses healthy tooth.

How should a broken mercury thermometer be cleaned?

Keep away, prevent others entering, ventilate safely outdoors and seek local spill guidance. Never vacuum, sweep or pour it down a drain. Cleanup depends on quantity and surface; large, uncertain, absorbent-surface or already-vacuumed spills need professional advice. Follow approved containment and disposal, not a general instruction to put the material in household rubbish.

Is an intact mercury thermometer the same as a spill?

No. Sealed mercury is a different situation from a damaged device releasing vapour. Store fragile items safely and choose a mercury-free replacement. If a device breaks or you cannot identify the liquid, keep away and obtain advice instead of testing it by touching, heating or smelling it.

Does a broken fluorescent bulb need the same cleanup?

No. Follow the bulb-specific instructions. Leave and air the room outdoors for 5–10 minutes, switch off forced-air heating or cooling and do not start by vacuuming. An appropriate adult should follow the full collection and local disposal guidance while the pregnant person, children and pets remain away.

Can work or a skin cream cause exposure?

Yes, depending on the substance and task or product. Occupational health can review controls and monitoring rather than assuming every worker must leave. Mercury-containing skin products should be stopped; wash affected skin, obtain medical advice and prevent household contamination from shared items.

Should I get tested or buy a detox after a fish meal?

Not routinely. A clinician decides whether the exposure history warrants testing and which sample and timing are useful. One fish meal is not proof of harm. Commercial detox, home tests and unsupervised chelation can mislead or cause harm; seek qualified exposure advice instead.

When is help urgent?

Get immediate medical or poison-service advice after a possible harmful exposure and emergency assessment if poisoning is suspected, without waiting for symptoms. Severe breathing difficulty, a seizure, fainting or loss of consciousness, marked confusion or rapid deterioration need emergency services. Do not drive yourself, induce vomiting or re-enter the contaminated area.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
